title: Make the bad patch finder's chain enumeration linear in the work it keeps, with identical output
body: **What changes.** Two changes inside `BadPatchFinder::FindBadPatchesGeneral` and nothing else, and a third that repairs a crash. A chain prefix that can never be emitted is no longer extended, and the greedy cover's frequency table becomes a vector indexed by patch number instead of a map rebuilt from nothing on every pass. The c stage, untouched against changed, on the quiet bench. One pair of bars per seed on a logarithmic axis, with the factor over each pair. **Why.** On a large tree the stage does not finish. When the build loop meets a bad patch or a repeat it stops assembling that chain, but the odometer goes on advancing its last index, so every suffix of an already dead prefix is enumerated one at a time and rejected for the reason the prefix was rejected for. On one tree that is 51,500,264,151 steps where 946,327 are kept. **That the output does not move.** Byte equality of everything the downstream writes, on fifteen growth trees of two scrolls. Seven trees of the first scroll: 585 files of 585 identical on six of them, and 40 of 40 on the seventh, the one where the baseline needed 6 hours 18 minutes. Eight trees of a second scroll, three arm pairings each: 936 files written by the downstream, none differing. On the first six the whole standard output of the stage is the same line for line, the longest 2,914,773 lines. **What it is worth.** One row per growth tree, on an idle machine, four threads, one run at a time, each on a fresh copy. The factor is the smallest second of one arm over the smallest of the other: | growth tree | baseline | with the two changes | factor | |---|---|---|---:| | seed40, 14,959 patches | 7,094.8 s, 1 run | 34.5 s, 3 runs | 205.65x | | seed38 | 7,930.6 s, 1 run | 56.6 s, 3 runs | 140.12x | | seed26, 9,512 patches | 49.4 s, 2 runs | 47.4 s, 3 runs | 1.04x | The factor column is the smallest second of each arm, which is the column `quiet-bench/evidence/c2-factor.csv` writes. Taking the median of each arm instead gives about 200 and about 130 for the two large trees, and the section below gives both readings and says which to prefer. The baseline of all three rows already carries the four changes of the pull request this one is stacked on, so the factor is this pull request's own and not theirs. There is no average across the trees. Two things belong beside the table rather than in a file. On the small tree these changes are worth four per cent: the two hundred times is on the trees where the enumeration is the whole cost. And for 1,572 s of seed38's single baseline run, 19.8 per cent of its wall clock, another tool of ours was reading files on the same machine, so 140.12 is an upper bound, while seed40's baseline was disturbed for 24 s of 7,094.8 and its 205.65 is not. **How to check it yourself.** Build this branch and the branch it is stacked on, run mode `c` on a fresh copy of the same growth tree with four threads, and time both. Then run the stages after it on both arms and compare every file the downstream writes. They should be equal. --- `BadPatchFinder::FindBadPatchesGeneral` is the slowest stage for anyone iterating on the patch generator, and on a large tree it does not finish. This changes two things inside it and nothing else, and carries a third change that repairs a crash. The delivered output does not move. ## What is slow, and a profile points at the wrong thing On a tree of 14,959 patches, **91.50 per cent** of the stage is in this one function, and by source line about **80 per cent of the whole stage is the descent of a `std::map`**: 50.98 per cent on the right child step of the red black tree, 24.06 on the body of `_M_lower_bound`, 5.41 on the left child step. Reading that as «the map is the problem» would be wrong. **The map is being asked too many times.** After the first change below, the whole odometer with its map descents is **0.46 seconds** of that tree's stage. ## Change 1: a prefix that can never be emitted is not extended The enumeration walks chains of length 2 to 5 with an odometer over `indices[0..length-1]`: `indices[0]` runs over the indexed patches and every later index runs over the alignment list of the patch the previous index landed on. A chain is kept only when no element is a bad patch and no element repeats. When the build loop meets a bad patch or a repeat it breaks out of assembling that chain, **but the odometer goes on advancing its last index**. Every suffix of an already dead prefix is enumerated one at a time and rejected for the reason the prefix was rejected for. The change advances the odometer where the chain died and resets the indices below it. On the tree of 14,959 patches and 230,513 relation rows: | chain length | before | after | |---|---:|---:| | 2 | 460,985 | 460,985 | | 3 | 20,319,828 | 73,846 | | 4 | 983,163,150 | 130,903 | | 5 | 50,496,320,188 | 280,593 | | **total** | **51,500,264,151** | **946,327** | a factor of **54,421**. **The before column is counted by walking that tree's `rel.csv` exactly, with no run, because the untouched binary on this tree was stopped at 3,000 seconds inside the first three rounds; the after column is counted inside the binary.** On a smaller tree where both can be done the two methods agree to the step, 10,761,063 each. The cost grows with the mean fan out of the alignment map to the power length minus one, and `AugmentAlignmentMap` makes that map symmetric, so on a tree where a patch has thirty alignments rather than five the fourth power is the whole story. ## Change 2: the cover's frequency table is a vector With change 1 in, a phase timer put **252.96 of the remaining 277 seconds** in the greedy cover at the end of the same function, which rebuilds a `std::map` of counts from nothing on each of 12,628 passes. It is now a vector indexed by patch number, cleared per pass. Scan order and comparison are untouched, which is why the chosen cover does not move. ## What the baseline already carries, measured tonight and not quoted from prose The untouched binary of every table below is the `corrected` series, and that series already contains four changes to this same function proposed on 12 September: a dead array switched off, a render state cleared per touched cell instead of wholesale, the normals precomputed, and the two loops parallelised. **Their own prepared text claims seventeen times and its study no longer exists**, so we re measured what they are worth, on one tree, on an idle machine: | ratio | median over median | the runs behind it | |---|---:|---| | the series **without** those four over the series with them | **31.11 times** | 1,548.2 to 1,675.7 s over 49.4 to 51.8 | | the two changes of this pull request, on the same tree | **1.05 times** | 49.4 to 51.8 over 47.4 to 48.6 | | all six together | **32.59 times** | 1,548.2 to 1,675.7 over 47.4 to 48.6 | Four threads, one run at a time, the machine between 0.05 and 0.12 cores busy of 24 before each, on a tree of 9,512 patches and 21,436 relation rows. Two of the runs behind this table had a 24 to 25 s burst of one core fall inside them, one of the two runs of the series with the four changes and one of the three without; none of the runs of this pull request's own arm. The burst was a watcher left over from another job of ours relaunching work that was already finished. Recomputed without those two runs the three ratios read 30.14, 1.07 and 32.32. Every one of those moves is smaller than the spread each arm already carries, 8.2 per cent of the smallest in the slow arm and 4.9 in the fast one, and the disturbed run in the denominator is the faster of its two, so the burst is not what makes the ratio. The table keeps the figures over every run that finished, and both sets are in the measurement notes that travel with this text. **One tree**: the same measurement on the large trees was not made, because at this factor it came to more than sixty hours each for a number this table already gives. So the honest shape of it: **on this small tree the two changes of this pull request are worth about five per cent, and everything else is the earlier work.** What they are worth is on the large trees, below. ## What the two changes buy Wall clock of mode `c`, four threads, on a fresh copy of each growth tree, against the untouched binary on the same tree. | tree | patches | relation rows | untouched | change 1 | changes 1 and 2 | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 14,959 patches | 14,959 | 230,513 | 7,251 s | 289.1 s | **34.9 s** | | 18,463 patches | 18,463 | 284,922 | 8,300 s | 472.7 s | **54.4 s** | | 22,205 patches | 22,205 | 304,256 | 7,808 s | 605.5 s | **63.0 s** | The three together go from 23,359 seconds to 152.3. Those three pairs were taken on a machine that was carrying other work, which is the weaker kind of measurement and is why **two of the three have since been taken again with nothing else running**. On an idle machine, four threads, one run at a time, 0.05 to 0.14 cores busy of 24 before each run: | tree | arm | runs | seconds | spread | |---|---|---:|---|---| | 14,959 patches | untouched | 1 | 7,094.8 | not measurable, one run | | 14,959 patches | with both changes | 3 | 35.6, 35.5, 34.5 | 1.1 s, 3.19 per cent of the smallest | | 22,205 patches | untouched | 1 | 7,930.6 | not measurable, one run | | 22,205 patches | with both changes | 3 | 62.2, 56.6, 61.2 | 5.6 s, 9.89 per cent of the smallest | **On the quiet machine the two trees give about two hundred times and about one hundred and forty.** Taking the median of each arm, 7,094.8 over 35.5 is **199.9** and 7,930.6 over 61.2 is **129.6**; taking the smallest of each, 205.65 and 140.12. The shared machine had given 207.8 and 123.9 for the same two trees, so the two ways of measuring agree to **4.0 per cent** on one and **4.6** on the other, and the quiet figures are the ones this text stands behind. One thing about the second of those untouched runs has to be said rather than left in a file. It ran for 7,930.6 s, and for **1,572 s of that, 19.8 per cent of its wall clock**, a tool of ours was reading files on the same machine, off and on, twice for minutes at a time. It is the largest disturbance on any run of this bench. It can only have made the untouched arm slower, which makes 129.6 an upper bound rather than a figure to defend, and the other tree, whose untouched run was almost undisturbed, gives 199.9. The third tree's untouched arm was not re measured at all. **About two hundred times**: 199.9 taking the median of each arm, which is the shape every other factor in this text uses, and 205.65 taking the smallest of each. The shared machine gave 207.8 for the same tree, so the two agree to four per cent, and the quiet figure is the one to use. Of those four runs three had the machine to themselves; the untouched one had a single 24 second burst of one core inside it, left by a watcher of another job of ours, which is 0.003 of its wall clock against four working threads. On a fourth tree of 26,947 patches and 457,647 relation rows the untouched stage took **22,699 seconds, 6 hours 18 minutes**, and the changed one **128.0 seconds** on a copy of the same tree. ## On small trees, and one measurement we cannot explain **The reference scroll, where every tree is a ribbon.** PHerc0139 is the scroll we hold a segmentation of, and every growth tree we have of it has a fan out between 4.7074 and 4.9490, so the enumeration this pull request attacks is already cheap there and there is little for it to save. That makes it the right place to ask the question upstream will ask: does this cost anything where it does not help. Seven distinct trees, 392 to 15,338 patches, **four runs of each arm on each tree**, each run on its own fresh working copy, arms interleaved so that drift falls on all of them. Three arms: the untouched binary, the untouched binary plus the orphan guard alone, and the untouched binary plus the guard and both changes. Below, the median of four against the median of four, and beside it whether the two arms' four run ranges overlap at all, because a ratio between two arms whose ranges touch is not a measured difference. | tree | patches | untouched over both changes | ranges overlap | the guard alone | overlap | |---|---:|---:|---|---:|---| | A | 392 | 1.034 | yes | 0.750 | no | | repeat | 7,854 | 0.990 | yes | 1.034 | yes | | S | 14,583 | 0.998 | yes | 0.895 | yes | | D450 | 15,117 | 1.010 | yes | 0.978 | yes | | C | 15,231 | **1.051** | no | 0.778 | no | | P2 | 15,338 | **1.125** | no | 1.003 | yes | | D150 | 15,183 | **1.290** | no | 0.935 | no | Read it in two halves, because they say different things. **The pull request as a whole never costs time on this scroll.** On four of the seven trees the four runs of each arm cannot tell the arms apart, and on the other three the changed binary is faster and the ranges do not touch: 1.051, 1.125 and 1.290. There is no tree of the seven on which the untouched binary is faster by more than the runs' own spread. **The orphan guard alone does cost time, and it is honest to say so.** On the smallest tree it is 1.33 times slower, on tree C 1.29 times, on D150 1.07, and on those three the ranges do not touch. The guard adds a check the untouched binary does not make. Taken against the guard rather than against the untouched binary, the two changes of this pull request pay that back and more: 1.379, 1.351, 1.379 and 1.122 on A, C, D150 and P2, with no overlap on any of those four. One caveat on all fourteen numbers, and it is why they are given as ratios of medians with their ranges rather than as timings. These runs were taken on a machine carrying other work, up to 12.1 cores busy of 24 at the widest reading, unlike the measurements on the other scroll above, which were taken with the machine to itself. The overlap column is the guard against reading too much into any single ratio here. A first measurement on a loaded machine showed the changed binary 18 per cent slower on one ribbon; the quiet re measurement does not reproduce it. Both sets, with the machine each was taken on: | tree of 9,512 patches | cores busy of 24 | untouched | with both changes | |---|---|---|---| | first, a loaded machine | 6.1 to 8.3 | 39.0 to 39.8 | 45.9 to 47.2 | | again, an idle machine | 0.05 to 0.12 | 51.8 and 49.4 | 47.4, 48.6, 48.3 | On the quiet machine the changed binary is **about 4 per cent faster** on that tree. The untouched column is what moved between the two, not the changed one. ## The output does not move Both changes were accepted only on byte equality of everything the downstream writes, not the delivered sheets alone. - **Six trees of the first scroll**: the whole downstream on a fresh copy of each, for each arm, against sha256 taken before the first compile. **585 files, 585 identical.** Also the **whole standard output of the stage, line for line**, on all six in both arms, the longest 2,914,773 lines. - **A seventh tree of the same scroll**, the one where the untouched binary needed 6 hours 18: **40 files of 40 identical**, the ten delivered sheets among them. So **seven trees of the first scroll in all**, not eight. - **Eight trees of a second scroll**, three arm pairings each: **936 files written by the downstream, 936 identical, none differing.** The input trees the arms share were checked unchanged separately, so the 936 are comparisons of what the chain wrote and nothing else. ## A companion fix, included here `patches/corrections/00007`, one file, 35 lines. `patches` is keyed by the `patch_.bin` files on disk; the alignment map is keyed by `rel.csv` plus the reverse edges `AugmentAlignmentMap` inserts, and that function inserts every alignment target as a key without checking the target was loaded. So a chain can be assembled through a patch that has alignments and no geometry, and `patches->at(p)` throws `std::out_of_range`. The guard refuses such a chain **where the chain is assembled**, not at the call that throws, which is one of three that would, and it counts and prints what it refused. On the tree where this happens it reports `chains=202 patches=73` at length 2, `178`/`58` at length 3 and `83`/`32` at length 4, and the stage runs on. On trees without such ids it reports zero at every length and the output does not move at all: byte identical, on every file the downstream writes. **Its time does move, and we would rather say so than have you find it.** The guard adds a `count()` to the loop that assembles chains, and on a scroll where that loop is most of the stage it shows. Measured with four runs of each arm on seven trees of a scroll of ribbons, the guard alone is slower than the untouched binary on three of them by more than either arm's spread: 1.33 times on a tree of 392 patches, 1.29 on one of 15,231, 1.07 on one of 15,183; on the other four the runs cannot tell the arms apart. Those are the same seven trees as the table above, and the two changes of this pull request more than cover that cost, 1.379, 1.351, 1.379 and 1.122 against the guarded arm with no overlap. Three single runs on the other scroll, 55 against 55 seconds, 81 against 78 and 53 against 49, had been read as no cost; one run an arm has no spread to read a difference against, and four have. How that tree came to exist is the subject of the issue this pull request accompanies.
